summary: Adjunctive hypnosis for clinical pain (2024 meta-analysis, n=6078 across 70 studies): small additional analgesic effect when added to usual care (MD ~−6.9 to −8.8 on 0-100), medium when added to education/medicines for chronic pain. Overall evidence certainty VERY LOW. No added benefit over psychological interventions alone at post-treatment.
content: Adjunctive hypnosis for clinical pain, 2024 systematic review + meta-analysis (PMC11390056, Pain journal). 7 databases to Jan 2024. 70 studies pooled, n=6078. Random-effects. Hypnosis adjunctive to usual care: small additional analgesic effect — chronic pain MD −8.2 [−11.8,−1.9]; medical procedures/surgical pain MD −6.9 [−10.4,−3.3]; burn wound care MD −8.8 [−13.8,−3.9]. Adjunctive to education: medium effect for chronic pain (MD −11.5) but not postsurgery. Adjunctive to psychological interventions: NO additional pain reduction post-treatment for chronic pain (MD −0.6, NS), small effect at 3 months only (MD −2.0). Adjunctive to medicines: medium effect for chronic pain (MD −13.2). KEY: 'overall evidence certainty is very low; therefore, there is still uncertainty about the analgesic effects of adjunctive hypnosis.' KEY for state debate: shows hypnosis has REAL but modest analgesic effects — consistent with both 'real phenomenon' and 'expectancy-driven' readings; the small effect over active psychological controls is awkward for strong-state readings.
